messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 40
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 37

He is 40 years old, married, and works as a software engineer, a job that once fit him well because it let him spend long hours focused on details and solving problems that had clear answers. Before the disaster, he describes himself as steady and practical, the kind of person who kept routines, planned carefully, and rarely let stress spill over into the rest of his life. He and his wife had been building a comfortable life together, with predictable weekdays and quiet weekends, and he had expected that the future would continue in that same measured way.

That changed the night the earthquake struck. He remembers first noticing the odd stillness, then the sudden violent movement, as if the ground had become unstable beneath everything he trusted. He was at home with his wife when the shaking began, and in the confusion he felt his body move before his mind could organize what was happening. Cabinets flew open, objects crashed to the floor, and the walls made alarming sounds that he later struggled to explain without feeling the same surge of fear. He thinks most about his wife’s face in that moment—wide-eyed, frightened, close enough to touch and yet suddenly unreachable. The minutes felt endless. He later describes them not as a memory but as a sequence of images and sounds that still come back too quickly: the roar, the dust, the darkness, the sense that the building might collapse before he could get both of them out.

In the days that followed, he functioned because he had to. He helped with damage control, checked on family members, and tried to stay useful, but he noticed that his mind kept snapping back to the disaster without warning. At first he told himself this was normal. He assumed the fear would settle once the immediate danger passed. Instead, the world began to feel different. He became alert to every small vibration, every heavy truck going by, every creak in the building at night. If a door slammed or a dish broke, he felt his heart race before he could think. He started sleeping lightly and waking often, listening for sounds that might mean danger. When he did fall asleep, he sometimes jolts awake with the impression that the room is moving.

As a software engineer, he is used to concentration and long stretches of problem-solving, but after the earthquake his attention becomes fragile. He sits at his computer and loses his place in code, rereads the same lines, and finds himself staring at the screen while his mind drifts back to the moment the floor shook. Meetings that once felt routine now leave him drained. He says he can still do the work, but it takes more effort, and he is frustrated by how much energy it costs to appear normal. He avoids news clips and social media posts about disasters, and even casual conversations about the event make him tense. He notices himself stepping back from certain places, especially tall buildings and crowded indoor spaces, and he checks exits in a way that feels automatic rather than deliberate. When his wife asks if he is all right, he often says yes because it seems easier than trying to explain how close the fear still feels.

He also feels a kind of guilt that is harder for him to name. He was safe, and his home was mostly repairable, yet he finds himself thinking of others who lost more. At times he feels ashamed of how much the event still affects him, as if he should have moved on by now. This makes him withdraw. He becomes quieter at home, less patient, and more easily irritated when small things go wrong. His wife notices that he is present but not fully relaxed, as though part of him is still listening for danger. He misses the version of himself who could laugh easily and sleep through the night.

Over time, he has come to recognize that the disaster did not end when the shaking stopped. It lives in his body in the quickened pulse, the stiff shoulders, the sudden startle. It lives in his mind in the images that return without invitation and in the careful ways he now moves through the world. He still goes to work, still comes home to his wife, still completes the tasks that hold his life together, but he does so with a persistent sense of being on guard, as if safety is something temporary that could vanish again without warning.
